newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-FALDO, WOOSNAM UNFAZED BY U.S. OPEN COURSE.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-FALDO, WOOSNAM UNFAZED BY U.S. OPEN COURSE.

text.p: Nick Faldo and Ian Woosnam, two of Europe's top prospects in this week's U.S. Open, were relaxed and confident on the eve of the year's second major championship.
The two Britons, both Masters champions, did not seem at all intimidated by the longest course in the championship's history -- the 7,213-yard, par-70 Blue Course at Congressional Country Club.

While Congressional's exceptional length, thick rough and four water holes had many other players gripping their clubs with white knuckles, Faldo and Woosnam seemed unfazed about tackling the treacherous track.

"It's just a very good, long, solid, honest, it's-all-in- front-of-you golf course," said Faldo, who has won three Masters and three British Opens and dearly wants to add the U.S. Open title to his impressive record.
"There are no surprises, no trick holes. It's a good solid golf course," Faldo added, perhaps with a touch of whistling past the graveyard.

"It's one of the best golf course I've played in a long time," said Woosnam, the 1991 Masters champion, who won the last European tour event he played, the Volvo PGA Championship, and was second in his prior tournament.
"The greens are good, and if they keep them like they are, it will be fine," added Woosnam, who also won a tournament in South Korea just before coming here.
Like everyone else, Faldo and Woosnam agreed that an accurate tee shot is the key to conquering Congressional, which has six par-4 holes longer than 440 yards -- including two converted par 5s.

"The round starts by hitting the ball on the fairway," said Woosnam, who once was one of the longest hitters in the game but is now overshadowed by the likes of Tiger Woods, John Daly and Greg Norman, who are also playing here.
"It's a demanding driving golf course," Faldo said. "The rough is very severe, as we all know."

However, Faldo said Congresssional, which is hosting only its second Open, was well suited to his game -- which he has been honing on the U.S. tour for three years in a determined effort to win the Open and the PGA Championship, the two major titles he needs for a "career" Grand Slam.
"I'm happy with the golf course," said Faldo, who usually hits the ball from left to right. "I think it's a fader's style of golf course, so I'm more than happy with it."
